about: TRAFFIC OF 793 - how many craft, of which classes, lie at each harbour, fish each coast, work each river, cross at each ferry, trade from each home port and go to war, by month, as a table the game reads (edit freely). Classes are ids in ship_classes_793.json; ports are ids in ports_793.json; regions are the ports' trade regions. Every count is a model estimate built from the evidence cited beside it: STARTING GUESSES TO TUNE, central values inside ranges of about x0.5 to x1.6. (?) = uncertain. LATER = evidence later than 793, used only as period practice.

units.counts: hulls (craft), afloat or drawn up, by day, real world
units.per_10km: hulls per 10 km of shoreline (sea coast plus estuary shore) or of navigable river
units.by_month: 12 values, January to December, mean for the month
units.profiles: share (0-1) of the peak, January to December

method: No ship counts survive for any port or river of c. 793. The numbers are built in five steps.

(1) Anchors, the size of each place: Dorestad's jetties 6-7 m wide and up to ~200 m long along at least 1 km of waterfront, ~2,000-3,000 people (?); Ribe's 40-50 plots laid out c. 705-710; Hamwic ~42-45 ha, Lundenwic ~55-60 ha; Reric with 6 boat graves; and the counts that do survive: 1-3 sea-going ships per great minster (S 86, S 29), 2 boats for Cormery (800), 10 taxable ships at Walenstadt (842/3, LATER), 2 seven-benchers per 20 houses in Dal Riata (Senchus).

(2) Throughput: ships in port at once = arrivals per day x mean stay (5-8 days at an emporium, 1-3 at a small landing); the season mean is ~0.65 of the July peak. Arrivals per year = (sea + river peak) x 0.65 x ~240 season days / stay.
(3) Household boats: local craft = households x the share owning a boat (~1/3-1/2 in coastal, marsh and river villages, less in towns); the same logic per km of shore gives the fishing densities.

(4) Season curves from period practice: Vegetius IV.39's closed sea (read in Carolingian copies), the Saint-Denis fair (9 Oct), ice months in the Baltic, Malaren and the Volkhov, the vintage and wine shipping, fish runs, and the voyage texts (Ohthere and Wulfstan, LATER).

(5) Cross-check: summed over the 50 ports, the central values give the totals in notes; the plan's ~130 simulated long-distance traders are about 2/5 of the home-based trading craft; the rest are an ambient layer (coasters, river craft, local boats, ferries) drawn near the player but not simulated as traders.

lay_up.practice: Sea-going trading ships stop long voyages in late autumn and are laid up at home: drawn up on the beach or bank on rollers, in boathouses (naust) in Norway (?), or moored in sheltered creeks in Frisia (?). Crews winter at home or, caught by the season, abroad.
lay_up.dates: long voyages ~1 April to ~1 November in the south, ~1 May to ~1 October in the north Baltic; coasting and river traffic continue at a low level all winter in the south
lay_up.evidence: Vegetius IV.39: sea closed 11 Nov - 10 Mar, risky 14 Sep - 11 Nov and 10 Mar - 26 May (read in the Carolingian period; Hrabanus Maurus' epitome c. 856, LATER); Wilfrid winters in Frisia 678/9 (Bede HE V.19); LATER: the Hanseatic rule, no sailing Martinmas (11 Nov) to St Peter's Chair (22 Feb)
lay_up.game: laid up at a port in month m = home x (1 - sea profile[m]) (river profile for river-only ports), drawn up

harbours.formula: present[m] = sea x sea_profile[m] + river x river_profile[m] + home x (1 - sea_profile[m] (river_profile for river-only ports)) + local + own. afloat[m] = (sea x sea_profile[m] + river x river_profile[m]) x the landing's afloat share + (local + own) x local_afloat[m]. drawn_up[m] = present[m] - afloat[m]. Visiting craft afloat: jetty or quay 0.9, riverbank 0.7, beach 0.3 (the rest beached or aground at low tide) (?). Laid-up home craft are counted drawn up.
harbours.fields: ports.<id>: sea = sea-going trading craft at the landing at the July peak by day; river = river cargo craft; local = fishing boats, ferries, lighters, errand boats; own = the lord's, abbey's or fort's own boats (classes: own_mix); home = trading craft based there, laid up there in winter; profiles = [a sea_profiles id, a river_profiles id (a sea_profiles id for northern rivers), a local_afloat id]; stay_days = mean stay of a visiting trader; present and afloat = hulls at the landing by month, Jan-Dec, from the formula (drawn up = present - afloat; recompute if you edit the peaks); basis = evidence | how the number was made. Classes of sea, river and local craft: class_mix of the port region's zone (zones).

template_by_kind_size._note: for a coastal port in north_sea_south (beach landing, temperate local boats); for ports added later. sea = base by size {1: 0.3, 2: 2, 3: 7, 4: 12, 5: 21} x kind factor (emporium 1.2, market 1, town 0.7, royal seat 0.6, monastery 0.5, fort 0.6, village 0.25); river ports add river_if_river_port x the river profile

dorestad.basis: Jetties 6-7 m wide, up to ~200 m long, built out as the river moved (Van Es & Verwers 1980); ~30 ha excavated 1967-77; ~80% of the pottery imported, mostly Rhenish (Badorf, Walberberg); silver-fir wine barrels reused as well linings; D.122 (779) names Dorestad among the toll places. Peak of the town c. 775-830. | ~100-150 jetty heads (1 km+ at ~8-10 m spacing (?)) x 1-2 berths = capacity ~150-300; ~30% used at peak. ~500 households x ~10% with a trading craft = ~50 home craft.

fishing.summary: In 793 fishing is inshore, estuarine and riverine: eels, flatfish, salmon, freshwater fish, smelt, shellfish and herring in modest numbers. Sea fishing for herring and cod on a large scale begins only c. 950-1050 (the 'fish event horizon', Barrett, Locker & Roberts 2004). Most of the catch comes from fixed weirs and traps on foreshores and rivers, worked from small boats or on foot at low tide. No fleets of sea-going fishing boats.
fishing.method: boats_per_10km = coastal settlements per km (marsh and estuary coasts every ~1-3 km; cliff and heath every ~3-6 km) x boats per settlement (3-10; 2-6) x 10. out_fair_day = boats_per_10km x the activity profile (share out on a fair day). The same boats fish, fowl and carry. Halve it on days of moderate wind; zero in a gale; zero where ice lies (lagoons Jan-Mar, Malaren and Ladoga Dec-Apr).
routine: out at first light, home by late afternoon; nets, lines and traps, never far from the shore
weirs and traps emptied at each low water, day or night, mostly on foot: 1-2 boats or people working each weir at low water
eel traps and weirs checked at dawn; the silver-eel run Sep-Nov on dark nights
autumn herring inshore with small nets in the southern North Sea, the Schlei and the Limfjord; no drift-net fleets (LATER, 12th c+)
line fishing for cod and saithe only on the Norwegian and northern coasts
night fishing with torches and spears is known later (?): none by default

rivers.summary: Rivers were the busiest waterways of the Carolingian north: Rhenish pottery, quernstones and wine went down the Rhine to Dorestad; grain, salt, wine and timber moved on every navigable river. Logboats, expanded logboats and flat-bottomed barges; downstream rowed or drifted, upstream towed from the bank, poled, or sailed with a fair wind.
rivers.method: craft per 10 km = (passages down per day x days on the reach going down + passages up per day x days going up) / (reach km / 10). Downstream 50-70 km a day; upstream 15-25 km a day; ~240-day season; 80% of craft return upstream. Worked example, Rhine Cologne - Dorestad (200 km): 600 passages down a year = 2.5 a day x 3.3 days = 8 craft going down, + 2 a day x 10 days = 20 going up, = 28 craft = 1.4 per 10 km on average, ~1.8 at the peak. Basis: Dorestad's 20 river craft at the peak / a 6-day stay = ~3.3 arrivals a day at the peak, ~2.2 on average x 240 days = ~520-600 a year.
routine: by day only; river craft lie at the bank at night
upstream: towed from the bank by 2-6 men on a line from a towing mast (Miracula S. Goaris, LATER: 'as is customary'), poled in the shallows, or sailed before a fair wind
downstream: drift with the current and steer with oars
tidal reaches (Thames, Seine to Rouen, Humber and Ouse): up on the flood, down on the ebb
stops at the toll places (Dorestad; Rouen, Amiens, Maastricht, Quentovic in D.122)
Sep-Nov: the new wine comes down the Rhine and Moselle; Dec-Feb: little moves in hard winters

long_distance.formula: plan (Plans/ai_fleets.md 1c): traders per home port = 0.4 x size^2 x a kind factor. The plan names no kind factors; these use the harbour kind factors (emporium 1.2, market 1, town 0.7, royal seat 0.6, monastery 0.5, fort 0.6, village 0.25). factor_793 adjusts single ports for what is known of 793; traders = round(plan_formula x factor_793).
long_distance.ambient: home trading craft not simulated as long-distance traders (coasters and river craft on short beats): drawn near the player from the harbour and river densities; ~1-3 coasters (5-12 m, 1-3 t, 2-5 men) per 50 km of populated coast in summer, beached at night at the nearest village (estimate)
long_distance.season: each trader laid up at home in winter (season.lay_up)
